title: Man killed in confrontation died of shotgun wound, post-mortem finds;
article: An Ottawaarea man killed in a confrontation with police north of Brockville Friday night died of a gunshot wound, a post-mortem examination has confirmed.

The province's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) yesterday identified the victim in the Forthton incident as 35-year-old Phillip Jeffrey Charbonneau, of Hammond, a small community in Prescott-Russell County just east of Ottawa.
According to court documents, Charbonneau had a history of traffic-related run-ins with police.
The post-mortem, conducted in Ottawa on Monday, found "the cause of death is consistent with a gunshot wound," the SIU said yesterday in a news release.

The unit, a civilian agency that investigates incidents involving serious injuries or deaths involving police, is also trying to contact an eyewitness to the incident who spoke to Sun Media on Monday.
But SIU spokesman Frank Phillips would not comment on the specifics of the ongoing probe.
"We want to interview everyone that we can," said Phillips.
Ontario Provincial Police officers shot and killed Charbonneau Friday night after he allegedly struck an officer with his pickup truck.

The OPP says two police officers suffered minor injuries in the incident, which resulted from a chase after Charbonneau allegedly bolted from a Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere (RIDE) check on the Hwy. 401 off-ramp at County Rd. 29 in Brockville around 11 p. m. Friday.
According to an OPP press release, a pickup truck approached the RIDE check after leaving the 401 and the adult male driver spoke to an officer and then fled the scene.
According to the SIU, the OPP's attempt to block the fleeing suspect "resulted in a collision between the truck and OPP vehicles."
Officers then "interacted" with the suspect and "at some point the truck struck an officer," the agency adds.
"Two officers discharged their firearms and the driver was struck at least once.
The male was pronounced dead at the scene," the SIU statement adds.
Julie Young, who lives in an apartment above the nearby Cedar Valley Golf and Country Club, on Monday told Sun Media what she saw unfold from that vantage point.
She added she had yet to be approached by the SIU in connection with the case.
Phillips yesterday could not say whether investigators in the case had spoken to witnesses at the scene, but added it is customary for the SIU to seek out nearby residents.
"I know we go banging on doors," said Phillips, who is also an investigator himself, although not working on this case.
"We probably won't go banging on doors at three o'clock in the morning."
Phillips could not say why Young had not been approached, but added the agency is attempting to contact her following her account in the newspaper.
He would also not comment on whether Young's account is consistent with any evidence investigators have gathered so far.
The SIU is still appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident to contact it at 416-622-1965 or 1-800-787-8529 extension 1965.
Witnesses are assured confidentiality, said Phillips.
The SIU currently has two "subject officers" in the investigation, as well as eight "witness officers."
Under the law, witness officers are required to co-operate with the SIU, while subject officers have the right not to speak to investigators, said Phillips.
Generally, subject officers who co-operate with the SIU speak to the agency with lawyers present.
Phillips would not specify whether any of the officers in the Forthton incident have spoken to the SIU yet.
Meanwhile, information obtained by Sun Media from a records check found that Charbonneau had not made any payments on a $5,000 fine he'd been handed in October 2008 for driving while suspended.
Police had pulled him over in the town of Alfred-Plantagenet, also in Prescott-Russell and east of Hammond, on Sept. 13 and charged him under the Highway Traffic Act.
A month later, he was convicted of the offence and handed the stiff penalty.
It wasn't Charbonneau's first traffic-related run-in with the law.
In April 2007, he was convicted of careless driving and fined $320.
A year later, in March 2008, Charbonneau was found guilty of speeding -- doing 96 km/h in an 80 km/h zone - and fined $50.
In May 2008, he was again convicted of speeding -- this time for doing 80 km/h in a 60 km/h zone -- and fined $90.
